claims.text: Quantitative grain-boundary character, phase-distribution, and defect-cluster descriptors can be integrated into a machine-learning-augmented simulation.

A machine-learning-augmented simulation using hierarchical-heterostructure descriptors can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior of HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately than conventional full-scale physics-based simulations.
The descriptor-based machine-learning simulation can make these predictions more rapidly than conventional full-scale physics-based simulations.
The proposed HfNbTiVAl10 specimens have well-characterized and repeatable microscopic phases, defect distributions, and grain-boundary conditions.
A limited dataset from targeted tensile and fracture tests is sufficient to train the proposed model to replace or supplement exhaustive finite-element or atomistic simulations.
Grain-boundary density, phase fraction, and spatial defect distribution can serve as quantitative mediating features.
Hierarchical-heterostructure descriptors capture microstructural variations that significantly affect load distribution.
Hierarchical-heterostructure descriptors capture microstructural variations that significantly affect crack propagation.
Adding these descriptors enables the machine-learning model to correlate microstructure more robustly with macroscopic mechanical properties.
Using the descriptor-enriched model reduces the need for computationally intensive simulations.
The enhanced machine-learning model will reduce predictive error by at least 20% relative to established physics-based simulations.
The enhanced machine-learning model will reduce computation time by approximately 50% relative to established physics-based simulations.
Full-scale finite-element or atomistic simulations for HfNbTiVAl10 require high computation time.
Full-scale finite-element or atomistic simulations have higher root-mean-square prediction errors for HfNbTiVAl10 than the proposed model.
The model may fail when its descriptors omit dominant physical mechanisms, including mechanisms active under high-temperature or dynamic loading.
Inconsistent microstructural features caused by sample variability may impair model generalization beyond the training conditions.
Prediction improvements depend on the quality and representativeness of the training data and on how well the descriptors capture the underlying physics.
